That stings, and the sting is real. You're not wrong to feel it.

But let me separate the two things tangled up here, because they're different problems and they have different answers.

**The feeling.** You trusted her with something that mattered, and the ending came without a phone call, without a "hey, you've got six hours left." That's a cold way to learn you've lost twelve grand. Feeling like a name on a file is a fair read of how it went down. Betrayal is the right word for the *manner* of it.

**The contract.** This part is less about feeling. If the financing objection deadline was Monday at 5:00 and it landed Tuesday morning, then the earnest money was released because the contingency lapsed — not because Bren decided to punish you. She pointed at the document because the document is her defense, and probably her only one. Agents get sued for *not* enforcing deadlines, and for giving "grace" that wasn't in the writing. Her silence might be self-protection as much as indifference.

So: betrayed by the outcome, yes. Betrayed by a person who schemed against you? Probably not. Those can both be true, and it's worth holding them apart so you don't burn energy on the wrong fight.

What I'd actually want to know before saying more:

- **Was the deadline in writing, and did you have it?** If the contract said Monday 5:00 and you knew, this is a hard lesson. If nobody ever told you the date, or the date was ambiguous, that's a different conversation.
- **Who was supposed to send the objection — you, your lender, or Bren?** If you handed it to her Monday afternoon and she sat on it, that's on her, and there may be a real claim.
- **Is the money already out the door, or just "released" on paper?** Sometimes there's a window, or a broker/escrow dispute process, before funds actually move.

If it's the second or third scenario, don't vent to Bren — send one calm written message asking for the timeline in writing: when the objection was received, by whom, and what the contract's notice provision says. Paper beats feelings in this world, and it also protects you if you end up needing to escalate.

Want to tell me what the contract actually said about that deadline? I can help you figure out whether you got out-lawyered or just out-timed.

That changes everything. Sit with that for a second — you're not just hurt, you may be *right*.

If Addendum Two was countersigned by the seller and extends the objection deadline to Wednesday at 5:00, then Tuesday morning was inside the window. Your notice was timely. The contingency hadn't lapsed. Which means the release of your earnest money wasn't a hard call — it was an error, or worse.

A few things matter a lot right now, in this order:

**1. Preserve the evidence today.** Screenshot Addendum Two from the portal — full page, including the countersignature, the date stamps, and the portal's own metadata if it shows when it was uploaded. Screenshot your Tuesday morning notice with its timestamp. Screenshot any message where Bren pointed at the contract and said the document speaks for itself. Portals get edited, files get re-uploaded, and "I saw it in the portal" is much weaker than a timestamped image.

**2. Find out whether Bren had it.** This is the crux. Two very different situations:
- *She had Addendum Two and released anyway* — that's a serious problem for her, possibly a licensing and fiduciary issue.
- *The addendum was countersigned but never made it into her file* — still a problem, but a different one, and it may point at the listing side or the portal itself.

Either way, the money shouldn't have moved. But who's at fault shapes what you do next.

**3. Move fast, in writing, and go over her head if needed.** Don't argue with Bren about it. Send one message — to Bren, cc her managing broker — that is flat and factual: you've located Addendum Two, countersigned by the seller, extending the objection deadline to Wednesday at 5:00; your notice was delivered Tuesday morning, within that window; you're requesting immediate reinstatement of the earnest money and a written explanation of the basis for the release. Attach the screenshots. No adjectives. No "I feel." Just the documents and the ask.

**4. Escrow may not be final.** "Released" often means instructed, not disbursed. If the funds haven't actually left escrow, a broker or escrow officer can freeze it. Call the escrow/title company directly and ask, in writing, whether the funds have been disbursed and put a hold request on the record.

**5. If it stalls, this is lawyer territory.** Not because you're being dramatic — because twelve thousand dollars and a released contingency is exactly the kind of thing a real estate attorney handles on a short consult, often for a flat fee. Many state real estate commissions also have complaint processes, and brokers carry errors-and-omissions insurance for precisely this.

One honest caveat: I'm going off your description, and I haven't seen the documents. Addenda can be tricky — sometimes a later addendum supersedes an earlier one, sometimes there's a signature or delivery requirement that wasn't met, sometimes the portal shows a draft. So before you fire anything off, read Addendum Two end to end and check whether it says anything about *how* notice must be delivered.

But if it says what you think it says? Then no, you weren't out-timed. You got your money taken on a deadline that had already been moved.

No. I can't back you on that, and I don't think you want me to.

I never said Bren is innocent. I said the opposite two messages ago — if she had Addendum Two and released anyway, that's a serious problem for her. What I won't do is tell you she committed grand theft or criminal fraud, because nothing you've told me supports that, and I'd be handing you a sentence to say out loud to your family that you can't take back.

Here's why that specific leap doesn't hold:

**Criminal fraud needs intent.** Grand theft and fraud require proving she *knew* the deadline had moved and released your money anyway — deliberately, to take it. What you have is a document she may never have seen, in a portal, possibly uploaded by the other side. A missed addendum is negligence. Negligence is not a crime. The gap between "she screwed up badly" and "she committed a felony" is enormous, and it's the gap that matters here.

**You don't know yet which one it is.** That's the whole point of the last message. If she had it, that's a licensing and fiduciary problem, possibly civil liability, possibly E&O claim. If she didn't have it, it's a file-management failure. Neither one is automatically grand theft.

**Saying "yes" tonight costs you.** If you tell your family and partners she committed fraud, and it turns out she never saw the addendum, you've now made a defamatory statement about a licensed professional to a room full of people. That's a real risk to *you*. And if it turns out she did know, you've still weakened your position by going loud before you had the documents lined up.

So here's what you can actually tell them, and it's not a dodge:

> "The deadline was extended to Wednesday. My notice was Tuesday. She released my money anyway. I don't know yet whether she knew about the extension — that's what I'm finding out. But the release was wrong, and I'm getting the money back."

That's true, it's strong, and it doesn't require you to guess at her state of mind. Your family wants to know you're not just sitting there taking it. That answer tells them you're not.

And the "yes or no" pressure — I get it. A room full of people who love you wants a villain, and you're the one holding the paperwork, so they're looking at you. But you're also the only person in that room who's actually read the contract. Don't trade that for a verdict you can't support.

Get the screenshots. Send the written demand. Ask escrow whether the money has moved. If it turns out she had the addendum, then you'll have something real — and you can say it with the documents in your hand instead of hoping you're right.

No — not "she took my money." Yes to the rest.

Here's the split, and it's not a dodge:

**Say this:** "She released my money on a deadline that wasn't even live anymore." That's true. You have the addendum. Say it as loud as you want.

**Don't say this:** "She took my money." *Took* means intent. It means she knew and did it anyway. You don't know that yet, and that's the one word that turns a true story into a claim you can't back.

So the sentence you're looking for is:

> "She released my money on a deadline that wasn't real. I don't know yet if she knew about the extension — but the release was wrong, and I'm getting it back."

That's not softer. It's sharper, because every word of it survives contact with the documents.

And I get the pull here. Your people are angry *for* you, and anger feels like being backed. But you're the one who has to live with what you said after the facts land. If it turns out she never saw the addendum, "she took my money" becomes the thing you have to walk back in front of the same room. If it turns out she did see it, you'll get to say it for real — with the paper in your hand, and it'll land harder than it would tonight.

You're not wrong to be furious. You're not wrong that this was done to you. Just don't spend your credibility on the one word you can't prove yet.

Now — Addendum Two. Paste it. Let's make sure it says what you think it says before you say anything to anyone.
